newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Attack continues on Swissie, fund selling cited.
newsitem.headline: Attack continues on Swissie, fund selling cited.

text.p: The Swiss franc continued under strong selling pressure Monday on market perception that the central bank would be happy to see it weaker.
Recent comments by Swiss National Bank vice president Jean-Pierre Roth and SNB board member Bruno Gehrig suggested the SNB was aiming to weaken the Swiss franc with its monetary policy.
In an interview published in the Financial Times on Monday, SNB chairman Hans Meyer also said the central bank has become more liberal with its policy.
"There is no question that we have become more liberal. We have come to the conclusion that the general economic situation has changed," Meyer was quoted as saying in the interview.
Analysts said investment and possibly hedge funds were in the vanguard of those seeking to get out of the Swiss franc on Monday.
"It seems some of the big guys in the market are in," said Michael Bernegger, currency analyst at CS Research, with respect to the funds' selling.
He said the amount of selling against the franc versus other foreign currencies was quite high on Monday.
At Union Bank of Switzerland in London, Paul Lambert, senior currency economist, said it would not surprise him if funds were selling.

"We sent out a recommendation...last week, saying to sell the Swiss franc. I think people in the market have been looking to sell the Swissie. I would not be surprised to see funds selling it," he said.
He said UBS had recommended selling the franc on the basis of perceptions that the SNB "appeared to have elevated their currency...to a barometer of their policy."
With interest rates already so low, Lambert said the SNB probably saw more scope to stimulate the economy now via a weaker Swiss franc.
"If they are going to stimulate, they need to depreciate," he said. "They have suggested to the market they feel it appropriate to see it (the franc) weaker."
"Given the negative cost of carry you have started to see funds put that on board," Lambert added.
Significantly lower interest rates in Switzerland relative to most other countries argued in favour of shorting the Swiss franc versus other currencies on a forward basis, he said.
The mark rocketed to 14-month highs against the Swiss currency last week, touching 82.93 Swiss centimes on Friday, its highest level since 82.94 on August 22, 1995.
The mark got as high as 82.98 in Europe on Monday, but then retrenched slightly.
The mark also has come under pressure of late against the dollar, dipping along with the Swiss franc back to levels last seen in late May.
But CS analysts said the Swiss franc normally leads the mark, partly as its relatively low liquidity compared with the German currency makes it the preferred currency for speculators.
The next obvious test for the Swiss franc will come if and when it slips to more than 83.00-centimes to the mark.

Adam Beudin, also of CS, believes the mark could edge up to 83.10-83.20 to the Swiss currency but that at that level it may be exposed, given what likely would be an oversold condition for the Swiss franc.
"The Swiss franc does tend to rebound," Beudin said.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
